subject: Cloud Computing
title: The Capital One Breach
description: A fast breakdown of The Capital One Breach for builders.

hook.text: In 2019, a former AWS employee exploited a misconfigured firewall and stole 100 million Capital One records.

buildup.text: The attacker exploited a server-side request forgery vulnerability in Capital One's cloud configuration.

discovery.text: The data included names, addresses, credit scores, and social security numbers — all stored in AWS.

twist.text: Capital One was considered a cloud security leader. They had invested heavily in cloud-native security tools.

climax.text: The breach proved that even sophisticated cloud users are vulnerable. Misconfiguration is an ever-present risk.

punchline.text: A cloud security leader got breached. Nobody is immune.

quiz.question: What was the root cause of the Capital One breach?
options: A misconfigured firewall exploited via server-side request forgery
An employee accidentally emailed all customer data
AWS disclosed Capital One's data to a third party

details.summary: In 2019, a misconfigured WAF on AWS allowed an attacker to exploit a server-side request forgery vulnerability and access over 100 million Capital One customer records including names, addresses, and credit scores stored in S3 buckets.
details.whyItMatters: The breach demonstrated that cloud misconfiguration, not cloud infrastructure weakness, is the real security threat. Shared responsibility failures have massive real-world consequences.
takeaways: A misconfigured WAF enabled a server-side request forgery attack
Over 100 million customer records were exposed
The breach was a customer misconfiguration, not an AWS flaw

faq.question: How did the Capital One breach happen?
faq.answer: The attacker exploited an overly permissioned WAF to perform SSRF, accessing the EC2 instance metadata service which returned temporary credentials. These credentials had excessive access to S3 buckets containing customer data. Multiple misconfigurations compounded the attack.

faq.question: What changed after the breach?
faq.answer: AWS introduced IMDSv2 requiring session tokens for metadata access, making SSRF attacks harder. Capital One paid an $80 million fine. The incident accelerated industry adoption of least-privilege IAM policies and metadata service hardening.
